lead: Water in a piston–cylinder at constant pressure, heated slowly, does not warm up steadily from ice-cold to red-hot. It warms, then boils at a fixed temperature while swelling enormously, then warms again. The same five states — compressed liquid, saturated liquid, wet mixture, saturated vapour, superheated vapour — appear in every pure substance, and their names, volumes and masses follow simple rules. Boiler designers, refrigeration engineers and steam-table users all work inside these states daily. This chapter names them, draws the constant-pressure path on the T-v and p-v planes, and collects every equilibrium state onto one surface in p-v-T space.
prereq: You need: system, property and state, and specific volume as an intensive property, from the basic concepts of thermodynamics.

blocks.text: A pure substance is matter whose chemical composition is the same everywhere in the system. Water is a pure substance; so is nitrogen. A glass of ice and liquid water is still a pure substance, because both phases are H₂O. Wet air is not, because the liquid water and the moist gas have different compositions.

A phase is a quantity of matter uniform in chemical composition and physical structure. Ice is one phase, liquid water a second, water vapour a third. A system may hold one, two or three of them at once.

Saturation is the state at which a pure substance can change phase with no change in temperature or pressure. At 101.325 kPa water boils at 100 °C; that is a saturation pair. Inside saturation, pressure and temperature are not independent — fix one and the other is fixed (the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, met with the thermodynamic relations, gives the slope of this link).

Five names cover the behaviour. Compressed liquid, also called subcooled liquid: colder than saturation at that pressure. Saturated liquid: exactly at saturation, about to boil, quality x = 0. Wet mixture: liquid and vapour together, 0 < x < 1. Saturated vapour: all vapour, about to condense, x = 1. Superheated vapour: hotter than saturation at that pressure.

sections.h3: Heating at constant pressure: the five states in order

blocks.text: Take 2 kg of water in a piston–cylinder at 101.325 kPa and 20 °C, and add heat slowly while the piston holds the pressure constant.

items: 20 °C to 100 °C: compressed liquid. The water expands only slightly, from v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001002 m³/kg to 0.001043 m³/kg. The heat added raises temperature; it is sensible heat.
At 100 °C: saturated liquid, x = 0. Any further heat starts boiling and the temperature stops rising.
Boiling: the temperature stays at 100 °C while the volume grows about 1600 times, from 0.001043 to 1.673 m³/kg. This is the wet region; the heat added is latent heat.
At 1.673 m³/kg the last droplet evaporates: saturated vapour, x = 1. More heat now raises the temperature again and the vapour becomes superheated.

blocks.text: v is the specific volume of the wet mixture in m³/kg; v<sub>f</sub> and v<sub>g</sub> are the saturated liquid and saturated vapour specific volumes at the same pressure, in m³/kg; x is the dryness fraction, x = m<sub>g</sub> / m, the vapour mass divided by the total mass, with 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

Figure 5.1.1 draws this path on the T-v plane, with v on a log scale so that 0.001 and 1.7 m³/kg fit on one page. The boiling stretch is the horizontal line at T<sub>sat</sub> = 100 °C; on the p-v plane the same stretch is a horizontal line at p = 101.325 kPa. Both stretches end on the saturation dome, the boundary of the wet region. Heat accounting for the three stages is in 5.4; the two ends of the dome are in 5.2.

sections.h3: The p-v-T surface and the triple line

blocks.text: The state postulate says that for a simple compressible substance two independent intensive properties fix the state. So all equilibrium states of a pure substance lie on one surface in p-v-T space. Compressed liquid and superheated vapour are single-phase sheets. The two-phase region is a ruled surface that joins the saturated liquid line to the saturated vapour line. Inside it, p and T are not independent, so the second property must be v or x.

Flatten the surface onto the p-v plane and the wet region becomes the saturation dome, crossed by a horizontal line for each constant-pressure heating. On the T-v plane the wet region is bounded by the saturated liquid and saturated vapour lines; each constant-pressure heating is a horizontal segment at that pressure's T<sub>sat</sub>. It is one object seen twice.

Ice, liquid water and vapour meet at the triple point of water: 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa. In p-v-T space the three two-phase surfaces meet along the triple line at that fixed temperature and pressure, because the volume may take any value between the three saturated volumes. Below the triple pressure water sublimes: ice turns straight to vapour.

items: Steam plants: the boiler drum and the condenser hold wet mixtures, so quality x sets what the plant can extract.
Refrigeration: the throttling valve leaves a wet mixture; the evaporator boils it off, usually to saturated or superheated vapour. The quality after throttling sets cooling capacity.
LNG storage: cryogenic tanks hold a boiling liquid near atmospheric pressure; a pressure drop causes flash boiling.

spec.aria: T-v diagram of water with specific volume on a log scale. The saturation dome peaks at the critical point, 374 degrees Celsius. A constant pressure line at 101.325 kilopascals rises through compressed liquid, runs flat at 100 degrees from 0.001043 to 1.673 cubic metres per kilogram, and rises again in superheated vapour.

examples.question: 2 kg of water at 101.325 kPa has dryness fraction x = 0.25. At this pressure v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 m³/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 1.673 m³/kg. Find the specific volume of the mixture, the total volume, and the mass of liquid and of vapour.
steps: Given: m = 2 kg, x = 0.25, v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 m³/kg, v<sub>g</sub> = 1.673 m³/kg at 101.325 kPa. Since 0 < x < 1, the water is a wet mixture.
Specific volume of the mixture: v = v<sub>f</sub> + x (v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>).
Total volume: V = m v = 2 × 0.419032 = 0.838064 m³.
Vapour mass: m<sub>g</sub> = x m = 0.25 × 2 = 0.5 kg. Liquid mass: m<sub>f</sub> = (1 − x) m = 1.5 kg.
Check: m<sub>f</sub> + m<sub>g</sub> = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2 kg, which matches the given mass.
examples.answer: v = 0.4190 m³/kg, V = 0.8381 m³, with 1.5 kg of liquid and 0.5 kg of vapour.
examples.check:
vf = 0.001043
vg = 1.673
x = 0.25
m = 2.0
v = vf + x * (vg - vf)
V = m * v
print(round(v, 4))
print(round(V, 4))
print(round((1 - x) * m, 4))
print(round(x * m, 4))

traps: Writing v = x v<sub>g</sub> for a wet mixture. Quality multiplies only the latent part, so use v = v<sub>f</sub> + x (v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>); the first term is small but it is never zero.
Thinking a two-phase system cannot be a pure substance. Ice plus water is a pure substance; moist air is not, because the two phases differ in composition.
Calling x = 1 superheated. x = 1 is saturated vapour, still on the boundary of the dome; superheat starts only above T<sub>sat</sub>.
Quoting both p and T inside the wet region as if they were independent. There T is fixed by p, so an extra temperature is either redundant or a contradiction.
Treating x as a volume fraction. It is a mass fraction, x = m<sub>g</sub> / m; the volume share of vapour is much larger because v<sub>g</sub> is hundreds of times v<sub>f</sub>.

quiz.q: Define a pure substance and give one two-phase system that is still a pure substance.
quiz.a: A pure substance has the same chemical composition everywhere in the system. Ice plus liquid water is a pure substance, since both phases are H₂O.

quiz.q: State the meaning of x = 0 and x = 1.
quiz.a: x = 0 is saturated liquid, about to boil. x = 1 is saturated vapour, about to condense.

quiz.q: Why does the temperature stay constant while water boils in a piston–cylinder held at constant pressure?
quiz.a: At that pressure the saturation temperature is fixed. The heat added during boiling separates the molecules from the liquid and pushes the piston back as the volume grows; it does not raise the temperature, so the mixture stays at T<sub>sat</sub> until the last liquid is gone.

quiz.q: Why is the specific volume of a wet mixture v<sub>f</sub> + x (v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>) rather than x v<sub>g</sub>?
quiz.a: Only the vapour fraction has the large volume; the remaining (1 − x) of the mass is liquid at v<sub>f</sub>. Taking x v<sub>g</sub> would drop the liquid volume entirely, which is wrong at small x and impossible at x = 0.

quiz.q: 1.5 kg of water at 101.325 kPa has x = 0.6. Take v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 m³/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 1.673 m³/kg. Find the total volume and the vapour mass.
A rigid vessel holds water at 101.325 kPa with specific volume 0.5 m³/kg. Is this state possible, and what is x?
quiz.a: 0.5 m³/kg lies between v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001043 and v<sub>g</sub> = 1.673 m³/kg, so it is a possible wet mixture. x = (0.5 − 0.001043) / (1.673 − 0.001043) = 0.498957 / 1.671957 ≈ 0.298.

quiz.q: Why is the meeting of ice, water and vapour a point on a p-T diagram but a line in p-v-T space?
quiz.a: On a p-T diagram both coordinates are fixed at the triple values, so it is one point. In p-v-T space the volume is free to take any value between the three saturated volumes, since the proportion of ice, liquid and vapour can vary; that free direction makes it a line.

beyond: Not for the exam. Supercritical carbon dioxide and ultra-supercritical steam plants run above the critical point, where the dome ends and the sharp boiling step disappears. Modern property packages replace the tables with international formulations of water properties, evaluated thousands of times per second inside plant simulators. Useful search terms: saturation dome, p-v-T surface of water, IAPWS-IF97.
